newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says "enemy of our time is inaction".
newsitem.headline: Clinton says "enemy of our time is inaction".

text.p: In a long State of the Union speech laying out second-term goals, President Bill Clinton on Tuesday issued a national "call to action" to improve education, balance the budget and reform campaign financing.

"We face no imminent threat, but we do have an enemy: The enemy of our time is inaction," Clinton told the joint houses of Congress in the ornate House of Representatives chamber and millions watching on television. "So tonight, I issue a call to action ... to prepare America for the 21st century."

As he described a rosy picture of a country enjoying a strong economy, with crime and welfare rolls down in a speech that ran one hour, much of the nation's attention was riveted on Santa Monica, California, where a jury was about to deliver its verdict on the civil trial of O.J. Simpson.
The White House feared -- unnecessarily, as it happened -- that the TV networks would preempt the speech for the verdict.
Its verdict that the Simpson was liable for the deaths of ex-wife Nicole and her friend Ron Goldman, both hacked to death in 1994, flashed on TV screens just as Clinton was finishing his speech.

Interrupted repeatedly by applause from members of Congress, Cabinet officers and Supreme Court justices arrayed before him, Clinton made a strong appeal for Democrats and Republicans to set aside partisan rancour and work together to help him make "the tough decisions of the next four years."

Departing from his prepared text, he said he knew it would not be easy but that one reason he was elected was "to support all of you without regard to party, to give you what is necessary to join in these decisions. We owe it to our country and to our future."

In the Republican response, Representative J.C. Watts of Oklahoma, the only black Republican in Congress, hailed Clinton's call for bipartisanship but rejected mere "feel-good" cooperation between the parties.
He said Americans want bipartisanship to be real.
"They don't want phony compromise, they don't want the kind of weak, back-scratching, go-along-to-get-along bipartisanship that makes lawmakers feel good, but gets bad results," Watts said.

Clinton denounced Republican efforts to amend the U.S. Constitution to require a balanced federal budget as the Senate prepared to debate the measure Wednesday, drawing a smattering of boos. He pledged to balance the budget without tampering with the Constitution.
"Whatever your view on that, we all must concede we don't need a constitutional amendment. We need action," he said as Democrats in the chamber clapped loudly.

Clinton spent the largest portion of his speech appealing for a "national crusade" to raise education standards to a level competitive with other industrial nations and "ensure that Americans have the best education in the world."
"Politics must stop at the schoolhouse door," he said.

He devoted a long section to foreign policy, vowing to pursue an expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation by 1999 and a "stable partnership" with Russia, which opposes NATO expansion. A Madrid summit in July is to start the process toward including former communist states of Central Europe into NATO.

Clinton also pledged to seek a "deeper dialogue" with China instead of isolating Beijing as some critics would like. He said he would go to China and President Jiang Zemin would visit the United States in pursuit of that goal.
He outlined an American role abroad far short of being the world's policeman but drawing the line against isolationism.

"America must continue to be an unrelenting force for peace -- from the Middle East to Haiti, from Northern Ireland, to Africa. Taking reasonable risks for peace keeps us from being drawn into far more costly conflicts later," he said.

The speech was a compilation of poll-tested themes from his 1996 re-election campaign. A year after he used the same setting to declare "the era of big government is over," his speech was thin on grand, large-scale initiatives in line with the country's perceived inclination for less government.

He performed the annual ritual enjoying some of the highest public approval ratings of his presidency -- 63 percent -- in spite of a nagging controversy over how he and his Democratic Party raised money for last year's campaigns.

Trying to deflate that issue and put pressure on the Republican-controlled Congress, he appealed anew for reform of how election campaigns are financed and set a specific date of July 4, the Independence Day holiday, for completing the work.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, was cautious on Clinton's challenge, saying it should first be determined what laws were violated last year. A team of FBI agents is investigating and congressional oversight hearings are planned.
"I don't see how you can decide what you need to do in terms of reform until you see how existing laws are being violated or abused," Lott told reporters before the speech.
Clinton was clearly hoping to make education his ticket into the history books.

He proposed $51 billion for education in the fiscal year starting Oct. 1, a 20 percent increase over current spending, to pay for education, training and tax cuts tied to education that are to be outlined in his budget blueprint to be sent to Capitol Hill for consideration on Thursday.

His education crusade involves a 10-point plan topped by setting up a programme in the next two years for national achievement tests in 4th grade reading and 8th grade math to ensure mastery of the basics. He would increase student access to the Internet.
